← Basement finishing bid calculator

How much to charge to finish a basement

Basement remodelers get shopped on a published $30 a square foot finished basement Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the bath or the egress. Eight hundred square feet of rec-room paint, drop ceiling, and carpet is a different job from 1,000 SF of legal living with a full bath, two bedrooms, two egress windows, HVAC, and a permit.

Open the free basement finishing bid calculator

Price the scope and the extras, not the $30 dump

A basement finish is finished square feet, then how much of the shell you are actually selling. Rec-room is paint, a drop ceiling, and carpet on walls that already stand. Framed-finish is studs, insulation, and drywall. Legal-living adds habitable-space extras. Drop ceiling is a grid. Drywall ceiling is hang and finish. Carpet is the cheap special. LVP is more hours and a higher invoice.

A rec-room is not legal living

The cheap special is almost always 800 SF of paint, drop ceiling, and carpet, no bath, no egress, no HVAC. A bedroom suite is a different crew month. Matching a per-SF number on a legal-living job is how a sold basement becomes a loss when the wet work and the egress eat the margin.

This is not waterproofing, a crawl, or a shower

Basement waterproofing is an interior drain, window wells, and a sump pit. Crawl-space encapsulation is a liner and access. A walk-in shower is a wet area, a slope, and glass. Drywall as a job is hang and finish gypsum. Flooring as a job is floor waste and tear-out. Interior painting is a coat. This prices a basement finish: finished SF, scope, ceiling, floor, and extras.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the basement finishing bid calculator. It is not a building-code determination, a waterproofing design, a habitable-space certificate, or a price you should copy onto a contract. Already holding a flyer number? See should I charge $30 a square foot to finish a basement for the walk-away price by scope.

Common questions

How much should I charge to finish a basement?

Charge from finished square feet, scope, ceiling, floor, bath, and extras — not a published $30 / SF special. Eight hundred square feet of rec-room paint, drop ceiling, and carpet is a different job from 1,000 SF of legal living with a full bath, two bedrooms, two egress windows, HVAC, and a permit.

Is a rec-room finish the same bid as legal living?

No. Rec-room is paint, a drop ceiling, and carpet on walls that already stand. Framed-finish is studs, insulation, and drywall. Legal-living adds habitable-space extras. Matching a per-SF special on a bedroom-suite finish is how a sold basement becomes a loss when the wet work and the egress eat the margin.

How do a bath, egress windows, and HVAC change a basement-finish price?

A half bath is a toilet and a sink. A full bath is a shower too. Egress windows, bedroom closets, a stair rebuild, a wet bar, HVAC extend, and a permit do not live in a published per-SF dump.

Is this the same as waterproofing, crawl-space encapsulation, or a walk-in shower?

No. Basement waterproofing is an interior drain, window wells, and a sump pit. Crawl-space encapsulation is a liner and access. A walk-in shower is a wet area, a slope, and glass. Drywall as a job is hang and finish gypsum. This prices a basement finish: finished SF, scope, ceiling, floor, and extras.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is. It is not building-code, waterproofing, habitable-space, egress, legal, tax, or financial advice. Verify every figure against your own invoices and crew times before relying on it.

should-i-charge-30-a-square-foot-to-fini.text:
← Basement finishing bid calculator

Should I charge $30 a square foot to finish a basement?

An owner brings you a Facebook post: “$30 a square foot, finished basement.” It reads like one number for any basement. It was priced for one scope — a rec-room: paint, a drop ceiling, and carpet on walls that already stand. Ask that same $30/SF to cover a legal-living bedroom suite with a full bath, egress windows, and HVAC, and it stops covering the job long before you get to the punch list.

Open the free basement finishing bid calculator

The number is scope-priced, not basement-priced

Using the calculator's own default crew rates (a $38 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin) on three named jobs, each priced from its own finished square footage, ceiling, floor, bath, and extras:

JobSF$30/SF specialWalk-away priceVerdict
Cheap special: rec-room, drop ceiling, carpet, no bath800$24,000.00$20,600.07Covers, +$3,399.93
Typical framed: framed-finish, drop ceiling, LVP, no bath, HVAC900$27,000.00$52,866.45Loses $25,866.45
Legal suite: legal-living, drywall ceiling, LVP, full bath, 2 bedrooms, 2 egress, HVAC, permit1,000$30,000.00$85,334.53Loses $55,334.53

$30/SF was never wrong. It was priced for the 800 SF rec-room job and it covers that job with room to spare. Nobody rewrites the flyer when the same owner asks for a bedroom suite instead.

Why the gap widens instead of scaling with the square footage

The flat rate moves in a straight line with square feet: 800 SF to 1,000 SF is 25% more dollars. The walk-away price does not move in a straight line, because a bath, two egress windows, two bedrooms, an HVAC extend, and a permit are not square-footage lines — they are their own tickets that a per-SF dump never carried in the first place. That is why a 25% bigger basement can need a 314% bigger check to actually cover it.

This is a scope question, not a size question

The trap is not "the basement got bigger." It is "the basement got a bath, egress, and code compliance, and the number I quoted from never had those in it." A remodeler who matches the flyer number on scope alone — without re-checking which of rec-room, framed-finish, or legal-living the owner is actually asking for — is the one who finds out the wet work and the egress ate the whole margin.

How to use the comparison

Open the basement finishing bid calculator, load the matching starting job from the "Choose a starting job…" preset list, and put the owner's per-SF number (times your finished SF) into "price you're considering." The calculator scores it against the walk-away price for the scope you actually priced, not the scope the flyer was written for.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to finish a basement and this calculator vs. Buildxact. It is not a building-code determination, a habitable-space certificate, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

Should I charge $30 a square foot to finish a basement?

Only on the cheap-special scope it was priced for. An 800 SF rec-room finish (paint, drop ceiling, carpet, no bath) walks away at $20,600.07, so $24,000 at $30/SF covers it. A 1,000 SF legal-living suite (full bath, two bedrooms, two egress windows, HVAC, permit) walks away at $85,334.53. $30,000 at the same rate loses $55,334.53.

Why does the same $30/SF number cover one basement and not another?

The per-SF number was set by the shell alone — paint, a drop ceiling, and carpet on walls that already stand. It carries no bath, no egress window, no bedroom, no HVAC extend, and no permit. Framed-finish and legal-living add studs, insulation, more drywall, and the habitable-space extras, which is why the walk-away price rises far faster than the square footage does.

How much worse does it get on a larger or heavier legal-living job?

Worse, because the gap is scope-driven, not just size-driven. A 900 SF framed-finish job (studs, insulation, drywall, no bath) already loses $25,866.45 against its own $30/SF number. A 1,000 SF legal-living suite loses $55,334.53. The dollar-per-SF price a homeowner anchors on does not move with the scope; the walk-away price does.

← Basement Finishing Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. tracking it in a spreadsheet

A remodeler pricing rec-room versus framed-finish versus legal-living scope usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a rate block per scope, a ceiling line, a floor line with waste, and a new section whenever the job needs a bath, egress windows, or a stair rebuild it did not have last time. Every formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping it wired together as the scope changes under you is the part that gets skipped when a homeowner needs a number today.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every line this calculator prices — shell labor and material by scope, a ceiling plane, a floor with waste, a bathroom kit, egress windows, bedroom extras, a stair rebuild, a wet bar, an HVAC extend, permit coordination, travel, overhead, and target margin. Building it means setting up separate rate blocks for rec-room, framed-finish, and legal-living, then remembering which cells to update every time the job's scope, ceiling, or floor choice changes — and adding a new block the next time a job needs a line item the sheet did not have last time.

This calculator keeps shell, ceiling, floor, bath, egress, bedrooms, stairs, wet bar, HVAC, and permit on one screen, already wired to the scope you pick. Changing scope, ceiling, or floor refills the starting hours and material for that choice automatically — a field you have already hand-edited is left alone, but nothing else silently keeps yesterday's number. The “same basement, three scopes” table re-prices your finished square footage under rec-room, framed-finish, and legal-living at once, and a saved bid or a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date are both one click, not a second document to build.

Building it means setting up separate rate blocks for rec-room, framed-finish, and legal-living scope, then remembering to update every formula that touches finished square feet whenever the job changes shape.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Re-price the same basement under all three scopes at once, so you can see where a rec-room rate would lose money on a legal-living suite before you quote it. Switching scope, ceiling, or floor in this calculator refills the starting hours and material for that choice automatically — a spreadsheet's cells stay whatever you last typed until you notice they are wrong. It also turns the same numbers into a printable customer proposal with a deposit split and a price-held date, and a shareable bid link that reopens the exact scenario for you or your crew, neither of which a formula cell produces on its own.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when the job has a wrinkle this calculator does not model — a walkout entrance, a second stair, a kitchenette, or a rate structure this tool's fields cannot represent. A spreadsheet you build yourself can represent any line item you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one basement finish, wired together so changing scope does not mean rebuilding the sheet.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser's local storage between visits, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page's URL hash rather than sending anything to a server.
